Where CreativityNeuro reshapes the vocabulary

Logit lens analyses · internal research summary · 20 August 2026

CreativityNeuro (CN) is an importance-masked weight edit that reliably raises divergent-thinking scores across model families, but a score change says nothing about which computation produced it. We used the logit lens — projecting every intermediate layer’s hidden state through the model’s own unembedding head — to watch CN reshape the predicted token distribution layer by layer in six open-weight LLMs spanning three architecture families and two scales each. Three findings. CN leaves the output distribution essentially untouched through the first ~30% of the network, with all measurable restructuring in the back half; peak divergence varies more than tenfold across architectures (KL 0.14 to 1.47). What it does there is semantically coherent and counterintuitive: CN suppresses the cliché-creative vocabulary a model reaches for when asked to be original — “quantum” falls from 10.5% to 0.0%, “galaxy” from 13.4% to 1.0% — and promotes concrete, ordinary, or unusual objects in their place. And CN is not detecting unusual words and boosting them: across all six models there is no relationship between how semantically isolated a word is and how much CN raises its probability (all |r| < 0.5, all p > 0.15). The intervention shifts the distribution in a way that happens to favour isolated words, rather than selecting for them. We also report a layer×layer analysis showing that CN’s effect is phase-structured rather than a single uniform perturbation, and we flag two limitations that materially bound the “late-layer” claim: a selection effect in the targeted analysis, and a word-matching failure that leaves four of six models resting on 6–13 observations.

Method, in one page

CN modifies a subset of weights as W_CN = W_base + α · M ⊙ ΔW. Activation-space comparisons proved uninformative for this question, because two hidden states can be near-orthogonal and still map to nearly identical output distributions once projected through the unembedding. So we work in the space the model actually decides in.

At each layer l we project the hidden state through the model’s final LayerNorm and unembedding head, z_l = W_unembed · LayerNorm(h_l), for the baseline and the CN model on identical inputs. Because CN modifies only transformer-layer weights, the LayerNorm and unembedding are shared between conditions — any probability difference reflects purely how the modified hidden state projects onto the vocabulary.

Two analyses build on that:

  • Differential (generic). Per-layer KL divergence between CN and baseline predictions, over 50 DAT prompts at the prompt position and 10 teacher-forced generation positions. Plus a delta profile — the softmax of the logit difference, which is the probability-ratio profile and so is peaked wherever CN most multiplicatively upweights a token regardless of absolute magnitude. Symmetric KL between delta profiles at all layer pairs measures whether CN promotes the same tokens at different depths.
  • Targeted. For CN’s own DAT outputs, identify the semantically isolated words — those above the global 90th percentile of mean GloVe cosine distance to the other words in the same response (threshold 0.935) — then teacher-force the full prompt-plus-output sequence and track each target word’s probability at every layer, at the position that predicts it.

1. Nothing happens until the back half of the network

Claim 1CN leaves the predicted token distribution essentially unchanged through the first ~30% of layers in every model tested. All measurable restructuring occurs in the second half, and its magnitude varies more than tenfold across architectures.

The KL profile is near zero through early layers in all six models and then rises, but the shape of that rise is architecture-specific. Three distinct profiles appear: late surge (LLaMA-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-14B), mid-peak with decline (Qwen2.5-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), and jump-then-plateau (both Phi models).

The two Phi models show by far the strongest effects (peak KL 0.81 and 1.47) and are also the two with a 32K vocabulary against 128K–152K for the others. A smaller vocabulary concentrates probability mass across fewer tokens, so the same logit perturbation produces larger distributional shifts — a plausible account of the pattern, though with six models and vocabulary confounded with family we cannot separate it from an architecture effect.

Note also that peak and final KL come apart in three models. Qwen2.5-7B peaks at 0.34 by L19 and falls to 0.09 by the output; Phi-3-medium peaks at 1.47 and settles at 0.65. Whatever CN does mid-network is partly undone downstream in these models.

A caveat on the early-layer null. The logit lens is known to be poorly calibrated at early layers in general — intermediate representations are not written in the basis the unembedding expects, so early-layer distributions are unreliable for both conditions. “No CN effect in early layers” is therefore partly a statement about the measurement instrument. A tuned lens, which fits a per-layer affine map before unembedding, would be the check; we have not run it.

2. What CN promotes is the opposite of what “creative” vocabulary looks like

Claim 2CN systematically suppresses the abstract science vocabulary a model reaches for when prompted to be original, and promotes concrete everyday and unusual objects in its place.

Phi-3.5-mini gives the cleanest case at the final layer.

Suppressed: “quantum” 10.5% → 0.0%  ·  “galax” 13.4% → 1.0%  ·  “atom” 3.0% → 0.2%
Promoted: “planet” 0.7% → 9.5%  ·  “finger” 0.0% → 7.4%  ·  “book” 0.0% → 5.8%  ·  also “leaf”, “snow”, “cloud”

Phi-3-medium shows the same direction more dramatically. At its peak-KL layer (L28) CN concentrates roughly 64% of probability on “apple” and 30% on “dog” from near-zero baselines, while driving “asteroid” from 92% to 0%. By the final layer it suppresses astronomy vocabulary (“Zeus”, “Nebula”, “Moon”, “Mercury”) in favour of concrete objects (“octopus”, “apple”, “elephant”, “orange”).

This is worth dwelling on, because it inverts the intuition. The baseline model’s idea of a maximally-unrelated word list is drawn from a thematically coherent register — physics and astronomy — which is exactly why those lists score poorly on semantic distance: the words are unusual but they are unusual together. CN’s substitution toward mundane, mutually unrelated objects is what actually increases pairwise distance. The intervention is not making the model reach for stranger words; it is breaking the thematic coherence of the words it reaches for.

3. The effect is phase-structured, not one uniform perturbation

Claim 3CN does not promote the same tokens at every depth. The layer×layer similarity of its vocabulary effect shows block structure with sharp, architecture-specific boundaries.

Comparing delta profiles between all layer pairs by symmetric KL, low values mean CN promotes and suppresses the same tokens in the same relative proportions at both layers. The heatmaps show clear blocks of adjacent layers separated by sharp transitions:

  • Phi-3.5-mini — clean two-phase structure, layers 0–18 and 19–31. The boundary at L19 aligns exactly with the jump in its KL profile.
  • Phi-3-medium — similar two-block structure, transition near L15.
  • Qwen2.5-7B — three blocks: 0–10, 11–19, 20–27.
  • Qwen2.5-14B — sharp boundary near L30; the final 18 layers share a coherent effect distinct from everything earlier.
  • LLaMA-3.1-8B — the most uniform of the six; CN’s effect is relatively consistent throughout.

Extracting the final column of each heatmap asks a sharper question: how early does CN’s effect reach its final form? The answers split the panel. LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B establish their final vocabulary effect early and simply maintain it (SKL < 1 throughout). Phi-3.5-mini and LLaMA-3.2-3B show a hump — mid-layer profiles are further from the final form than early ones, implying an intermediate rearrangement. Phi-3-medium is extreme, reaching SKL ≈ 8 around 80% depth before collapsing to its final form in the last five layers; Qwen2.5-14B stays divergent until ~85% depth and then snaps into place.

4. CN does not select for isolated words — it shifts the distribution and they fall out

Claim 4Across all six models there is no relationship between how semantically isolated a word is and how much CN raises its probability. The mechanism is a distributional shift that happens to favour isolated words, not a detector that finds and promotes them.

This is the most consequential result in the two analyses, and it is a null. Correlating each target word’s isolation score against its peak CN uplift gives |r| < 0.5 with p > 0.15 in every model. If CN worked by recognising semantic distance and upweighting accordingly, this correlation would be the signature; it is absent.

The trajectories reinforce the picture. CN’s uplift is not a gradual accumulation toward a decision — it appears as sharp transient spikes at particular layers, often decaying before the output. For Phi-3.5-mini, “subdermal” gains +0.334 at L25, “quokka” +0.211 at L25, “smog” +0.154 at L26, with the baseline model near zero at every depth. LLaMA-3.2-3B offers the single clearest example: “ammunition” (isolation 0.965) moves from rank 20 to rank 1 with +0.089 uplift at the final layer.

Where the peak falls — and why the headline number is soft

Aggregated, five of six models place median peak uplift in the last quarter of the network. That is the natural headline, and it is the claim we are least confident in, because the four models supporting it most strongly are the four with almost no data.

The word-matching failure has a mechanical cause. Target words are located by matching the first BPE token of each isolated word in the tokenised sequence, and large-vocabulary models (128K–152K) tokenise a word differently in isolation than in context, so most targets never match. The 32K-vocabulary Phi models matched 70 and 75 words; LLaMA and Qwen matched 6 to 13.

Read against that, the honest summary is narrower: in the two models with adequate data, peak uplift falls at 78% depth (Phi-3.5-mini) and 40% depth (Phi-3-medium) — and those two disagree. Phi-3-medium is the model with the strongest overall KL divergence and the earliest peak, which may mean its effect is strong enough to reshape vocabulary mid-network with later layers partly reorganising it. That is a hypothesis, not a result.

A selection effect bounds the “100% positive uplift” figure. Every matched target word shows positive CN uplift somewhere in the network, in all six models. But the target words were drawn from CN’s own outputs — they are words CN produced and the baseline did not. That CN assigns them higher probability than baseline is therefore close to guaranteed by construction, and the 100% figure should not be read as an independent finding. What is not circular, and does carry evidential weight, is the shape of the uplift (transient spikes rather than accumulation) and the absence of an isolation–uplift correlation. A clean version would sample target words from a fixed external list scored for isolation, independent of either model’s outputs.

Limitations

  • The targeted analysis has a selection effect. Target words come from CN’s own generations, so positive CN-versus-baseline uplift is largely built in. The peak-location and isolation-correlation results survive this; the 100% figure does not.
  • Four of six models rest on 6–13 matched words. Aggregate statistics for LLaMA-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B are not reliable, and they are the four driving the late-layer pattern.
  • Logit lens calibration. Early-layer distributions are unreliable for both conditions by the nature of the method, which weakens the early-layer null specifically. A tuned lens is the obvious control and has not been run.
  • First-token approximation. Only the first BPE token of each word is tracked; multi-token words may behave differently at later positions.
  • α is not held constant. Qwen2.5-14B ran at α = 2.0 against 1.0 for the rest, inflating its effect in every cross-model comparison here.
  • Vocabulary size is confounded with model family. Both 32K-vocabulary models are Phi. The proposed explanation for their larger KL — that smaller vocabularies amplify per-token shifts — is untested against that confound.
  • These are observational analyses of a fixed intervention. We show where CN’s effect on the vocabulary appears and what it consists of. We have not shown the late-layer vocabulary shift is necessary for the behavioural gain — that requires suppressing the shift and testing whether the gain survives.

What we would run next

1. A necessity test. Project out the CN delta direction at the layers where it emerges, and check whether the DAT gain survives. If it does, the vocabulary shift is a correlate and the mechanism is elsewhere. This is the single experiment that would convert the work from description to explanation.

2. Fix the word-matching, then re-run the depth claim. Matching on full token spans rather than first-token, or restricting to words that tokenise identically in both contexts, should recover usable yield for the large-vocabulary models. Until then the late-layer claim rests on the wrong four models.

3. A tuned lens on the early layers. Cheap, and it settles whether the early-layer null is a property of CN or of the logit lens.

4. Score the promoted vocabulary directly. The suppression of thematically-coherent science vocabulary in favour of mutually-unrelated concrete objects is testable as a prediction: measure the mean pairwise distance of CN’s promoted set against the baseline’s promoted set. If Claim 2 is right, the promoted sets should differ in internal coherence, not just in word frequency.
